pages.name: Which holds?
pages.task: A square frame and a triangle frame of pinned bars each stand on two supports. Push sideways on the top of each. Which one keeps its shape?
pages.why: Every joint is a pin, free to turn like a hinge. The square's four bars can all lean over into a diamond. So the square folds. Three bars of fixed length make one triangle and no other. So the triangle cannot change shape.

pages.name: Counting ways to move
pages.text: The triangle has 3 joints and 3 bars. It needs 2 × 3 − 3 = 3, so it holds. The square has 4 joints and 4 bars. It needs 2 × 4 − 3 = 5, so it is one short and folds.

pages.name: Lock the frame
pages.task: A square frame with a triangle roof on top has 5 joints and 6 bars. What is the fewest bars it needs to hold its shape?
pages.why: It needs 2 × 5 − 3 = 7 bars. It has only 6. So it has one way left to move, and its square part leans over. A diagonal across the square is the seventh bar. Then the whole frame is triangles.

pages.name: Grow the frame
pages.task: A frame of two square bays has 6 joints and 8 bars. How many more bars does it need to hold its shape?
pages.why: It needs 2 × 6 − 3 = 9 bars. It has 8, so it needs 1 more. That is a diagonal across the right bay. Each new joint brings two ways to move, so it needs two new bars. That is why a frame grown one triangle at a time keeps the count right.

pages.name: Off centre
pages.task: A frame spans 6 m between its supports. A 12 kN load hangs from a joint 2 m from the left support. How hard does the left support push up?
pages.why: The load is 6 − 2 = 4 m from the right support. Its moment about that support is 12 × 4 = 48 kN m. The left support is 6 m away, and its push must balance that moment. So it pushes 48 ÷ 6 = 8 kN. The right support takes the rest, 12 − 8 = 4 kN.

pages.text: A stretched bar pulls its pins towards each other. So its arrow at each pin points away from that pin, labelled pull. A squashed bar pushes its pins apart. So each arrow points into its pin, labelled push.

pages.name: Which is pulled?
pages.task: A triangle frame carries a load at its top joint. Which bar is in tension?
pages.why: The load presses the top joint down. That squashes both sloping bars. Squashed, they push their feet outwards. The roller cannot push sideways. So the bottom bar holds the feet together by pulling.

pages.name: The bottom bar
pages.task: At the left foot, the support pushes up with 5 kN. The sloping bar pushes into the foot with 10 kN, at 30° above level. What is the force in the bottom bar?
pages.why: The sloping bar's across part is 10 × cos 30° = 8.66 kN. It pushes the foot outwards. Its up part is 10 × sin 30° = 5 kN, which matches the support's push. The pin could push sideways too. But no other force on the frame pushes sideways, so here it pushes only up. So the bottom bar must pull the foot inwards with 8.66 kN. Its arrow points away from the pin, so it is in tension.

pages.name: A screw is a ramp
pages.text: One turn of a 20 mm screw's thread unrolls into a ramp 62.8 mm long. The ramp climbs 2 mm, drawn five times taller here. With friction ignored, a push along the thread lifts a load 31.4 times its size.
pages.alt: A screw 20 mm across, its thread wound round the shaft. One turn of the thread lies flat as a ramp 62.8 mm long that climbs 2 mm, its climb drawn 5 times taller. The load lifted is 31.4 times the push.

pages.name: A finer thread
pages.task: The same 20 mm screw gets a finer thread, with a 1.5 mm pitch. With friction ignored, how many times the push is the load?
pages.why: One turn runs π × 20 = 62.8 mm and climbs 1.5 mm. So push × 62.8 mm = load × 1.5 mm. The load is 62.8 ÷ 1.5 = 41.9 times the push. A finer thread lifts more for each push, but takes more turns. That is how a terminal screw clamps a conductor hard from a small twist. Left loose, it presses on less of the conductor, and the joint runs hot.

pages.name: Same count
pages.task: Two frames of two square bays each have 6 joints and 9 bars. Frame A has a diagonal in each bay. Frame B has both diagonals in its left bay. Which one folds?
pages.answer: Frame B, both diagonals in one bay
pages.why: The count says how many bars a frame needs, not where they go. Frame B's second diagonal locks nothing the first one had not already locked. So it is spare. Its right bay is a square with no diagonal, so it folds.

pages.name: A steeper frame
pages.task: A triangle frame on two supports carries 12 kN at its top joint. Its sloping bars are at 45° to level. What force is in each sloping bar?
pages.why: The two bars slope equally, so they share the load equally. Each bar's up part is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kN. The up part is the force × sin 45°. So the force is 6 ÷ 0.707 = 8.49 kN. Both arrows point into the top joint, so both bars are in compression. At each foot, the bottom bar then pulls with 8.49 × cos 45° = 6.00 kN.
